lines: Morgan Patel
+1 (555) 010-4410 | morgan.patel@example.com | example.com/code/mpatel
EDUCATION
Ridgeway University | Ph.D. candidate in Statistics | Metro City, USA | Sep 2021 - Expected May 2026
Ridgeway University | B.S. in Mathematics | Metro City, USA | Sep 2016 - May 2020
EXPERIENCE
Sunrise Bakery | Assistant Store Manager | Metro City, USA | Sep 2025 - Present
- Managed opening shifts and a team of 6 bakers and cashiers, keeping the store within its weekly labour budget.
- Ran daily stock counts and supplier orders, cutting unsold bread from 12% to 7% of production.
Northpeak Capital | Quantitative Research Intern | Metro City, USA | Jun 2025 - Aug 2025
- Built a short-horizon order-book imbalance signal for liquid index futures that raised the desk book's Sharpe ratio from 1.1 to 1.5 over 18 months of out-of-sample backtest after costs.
- Cut the signal's daily turnover from 34% to 21% with a cost-aware position smoother, keeping 90% of gross returns and lowering estimated slippage by a third.
- Confirmed the forecast gain over the nested HAR-RV baseline with standard Diebold-Mariano tests across the 30 indices.
- Joining 120 microstructure features point-in-time across six venues, deduplicating late prints and versioning each schema, built a feature store the team reused in two later projects.
- Annualized the signal's daily Sharpe ratio by multiplying it by 252 before reporting it to the desk.
- Documented the backtest assumptions, transaction-cost model and known failure regimes in the desk's research wiki, which the next intern cohort used to onboard in their first week.
Ridgeway University | Research Assistant, Statistical Learning Lab | Metro City, USA | Jun 2020 - Aug 2021
- Built the lab's simulation pipeline on the shared cluster, cutting a 2,000-run Monte Carlo study from 3 days to 5 hours, with every run reproducible from its seed and configuration file.
- Derived a variance bound for a sparse regression estimator; my proof tightens the previous bound by a log factor and is now Section 3 of a paper under review at JASA.
- Taught weekly recitations for 60 students in graduate probability, writing 12 problem sets and earning a 4.8/5 teaching rating.

- Released an open-source R package for high-dimensional covariance estimation while maintaining the lab's shared cluster, organizing the weekly reading group and grading for two courses, which was downloaded 3,000 times in its first year.
PROJECTS
Volatility Forecasting Study | Independent Research | Python, PyTorch | Jan 2024 - Present
- Beat a HAR-RV baseline's out-of-sample QLIKE loss by 7% on 30 equity indices with a temporal convolutional model trained on realized-volatility features.
- Cut forecast error from 0.20 to 0.15, a 33% improvement, by adding realized-volatility features and an asymmetric loss.
- Improved the model's directional hit rate by 6% on 30 equity indices, from 52% to 58%, with a temporal convolutional model.
Kaggle Market Prediction Competition | Team of 3 | Python | Mar 2023 - Jun 2023
- Placed 41st of 2,900 teams with a gradient-boosting ensemble on 300 engineered features, finishing in the top 2% of the private leaderboard.
- Cut validation leakage by switching to time-grouped folds, which closed a 0.02 gap between local validation and leaderboard scores.
- Wrote the team's feature-selection script using permutation importance, trimming 900 candidate features to 300 without losing validation score.
SKILLS
Programming: Python, R, PyTorch, Kafka
Methods: time-series econometircs, high-dimensional statistics, gradient boosting

items.says: Make the code link’s destination and purpose clear.
items.because: The URL does not indicate whether it leads to GitHub, a portfolio, or something else.

items.says: Consider adding LinkedIn if you use it professionally.
items.because: It can make your background easier for recruiters to verify.

items.says: Move Skills higher, likely after Education.
items.because: Python, R, and quantitative methods are important screening terms that should be easy to find.

items.says: Consider removing the repeated work locations.
items.because: All roles list the same city, so the locations use space without adding much information.

items.says: Add a concise, relevant dissertation or research focus if you have one.
items.because: It could connect your doctoral work to the roles you are targeting.

items.says: Make the bakery role’s relevance to your target clear through its results.
items.because: The role is less relevant than your quant work, though its leadership, budgeting, and inventory control are transferable.

items.says: Clarify the result of staying within the labour budget.
items.because: The bullet shows responsibility but not whether you met a target, avoided overspend, or improved on a prior result.

items.says: Define the comparison period or measurement basis for the unsold-bread reduction.
items.because: Readers may wonder what the percentages measure.

items.says: Specify the Sharpe ratios’ basis of comparison and the result’s scope.
items.because: “Desk book,” annualization, and how the signal’s contribution was isolated are unclear.

items.says: Define the turnover calculation and the comparison behind “keeping 90% of gross returns.”
items.because: Those metrics are ambiguous.

items.says: Clarify whether the slippage reduction uses the backtest’s cost model.
items.because: The review asks whether it is an estimate from that same model.

items.says: Give the significance result and clarify the forecast target and horizon.
items.because: The bullet needs more detail to support its inference.

items.says: Verify that standard Diebold–Mariano testing suits the nested comparison.
items.because: It may not be the right procedure in that setting.

items.says: Consider addressing multiple comparisons across the 30 indices.
items.because: Testing across that many indices may require it.

items.says: Fix the feature-store bullet’s grammatical construction.
items.because: Its opening participle does not connect cleanly to the main clause, leaving unclear who built the store.

items.says: Prioritize the feature-store bullet’s core contribution.
items.because: It combines data integration, data-quality work, schema versioning, and later reuse.

items.says: Make the feature store’s later reuse claim concrete.
items.because: The review asks for a clearer account of that result.

items.says: Correct or remove the daily Sharpe annualization claim.
items.because: A daily Sharpe ratio is not annualized by multiplying it by 252; under the usual independent-return assumption, the factor is the square root of 252.

items.says: Replace the reporting-calculation bullet with a research achievement.
items.because: As written, it could undermine confidence in the financial math elsewhere on the résumé.

items.says: Substantiate the next cohort’s onboarding result or prioritize more technical work.
items.because: The onboarding claim would be stronger with a specific, verifiable effect.

items.says: Name the relevant tools or cluster environment if space allows.
items.because: That would add technical detail to the simulation-pipeline result.

items.says: Clarify your individual contribution to the variance bound.
items.because: Readers may not know what tightening the previous bound by a log factor means.

items.says: Make sure the manuscript status remains current.
Give context for the 4.8/5 teaching rating.
items.because: Readers may wonder how many responses it reflects or what it measures.

items.says: Treat the problem-set count as secondary if space is needed.
Split or substantially narrow the final lab bullet.
items.because: It bundles a package release, cluster maintenance, reading-group organization, grading, and downloads.

items.says: Make clear that the download count describes the package.
items.because: The sentence structure leaves that relationship unclear.

items.says: Reduce overlap among the three volatility-study bullets and say whether they come from the same experiment.
items.because: They all describe results from a temporal convolutional volatility model on 30 equity indices.

items.says: State the QLIKE result’s evaluation setup and comparison clearly.
items.because: Without a clear distinction from the forecast-error result, the bullets can look inconsistent or repetitive.

items.says: Name the forecast-error metric, evaluation setup, and comparison.
items.because: The 33% forecast-error result uses a different metric from the 7% QLIKE result, but that distinction is unclear.

items.says: Explain why directional hit rate matters or reconsider the result.
items.because: Directional accuracy is not an obvious primary metric for volatility forecasting.

items.says: Avoid repeating the model type and dataset without adding information.
items.because: Those technical details already appear elsewhere in the project.

items.says: Explain the evaluation context and what the 0.02 gap represents.
items.because: The score scale and the effect of the change are undefined.

items.says: Clarify what “without losing validation score” means.
items.because: It is unclear whether the score was unchanged within a tolerance or merely similar.

items.says: Make the validation method consistent with the leakage-prevention bullet.
Do not list PyTorch and Kafka as programming languages.
items.because: PyTorch is a framework or library, and Kafka is a data-streaming technology.

items.says: Consider listing other relevant tools you have actually used.
items.because: Your experience suggests skills such as SQL, version control, or backtesting tools may be useful to list.

items.says: Correct the misspelling “econometircs.”
items.because: A skills-list misspelling can hurt credibility and keyword matching.

items.says: Consider replacing broad method labels with accurate, more specific methods.
items.because: Specific methods may better reflect your work and match the roles you are pursuing.
